title: How to manage your contact center day-to-day during the holidays
summary: One morning in mid-December, a workforce management (WFM) analyst pulls up the latest numbers and spots a problem: contact volume is well above forecast.
body_markdown:
One morning in mid-December, a workforce management (WFM) analyst pulls up the latest numbers and spots a problem: contact volume is well above forecast. A major carrier is running behind on holiday deliveries due to inclement weather, and customers want to know where their gifts are. By lunch, agents are bogged down answering the same question across channels, and the staffing plan put together weeks ago isn’t keeping pace.


Even a well-prepared contact center can’t anticipate every surprise, and shoppers might react to winter storms and last-minute promotions unpredictably. That’s why the teams that best manage the holiday rush tend to treat their original schedule as a starting point and adjust it as they go.


To close out our holiday contact center readiness series, we’ll walk through a typical workday during peak season, from the morning standup to the conversation analysis that determines tomorrow’s priorities, and outline how supervisors and WFM analysts can support both customers and agents alike.


## What should a daily contact center standup cover?


A 15-minute standup at the start of each day gives supervisors and the WFM analyst a chance to review what happened yesterday and agree on what to refine today.


Open with the previous day’s conversation analysis. In our example, yesterday’s data might have shown a small but growing number of customers asking about orders from the delayed carrier. Flagging that trend at the standup gives the team a head start before more customers reach out about it.


From there, decide which knowledge content needs immediate updating. If agents don’t have a clear answer about the delay, write one that covers revised delivery estimates and what customers can do if a gift won’t arrive in time.


That answer can go to AI agents as well, so they can resolve more order status requests on their own. The team may also adjust an escalation rule so customers with status or higher-value orders whose gifts are at risk of arriving late reach a human agent faster.


The standup is a good opportunity to check in on individual agents too. Supervisors can identify anyone who had trouble the day before, like a new seasonal agent who struggled with billing questions, and work with the WFM analyst to fit a short training session into a lower-volume window.


## How do supervisors monitor AI and human conversations live?


Once the day is underway, supervisors turn their focus to live conversations. Real-time trackers and alerts flag conversations that need intervention, such as a customer asking for a refund because a shipment is coming late. When an alert comes in, supervisors can coach the human agent, especially if they are seasonal, through the conversation or join it directly.


Supervisors should also keep an eye on AI agent conversations. If customers asking about the carrier delay keep requesting a person, the AI agent’s answer may be missing the right information. Long AI agent conversations with frustrated customers can point to an escalation rule that isn’t triggering as intended.


Supervisors can note these cases as they come up and share them with whoever manages the AI agent, so that person can update the answer or rule quickly.


## How do WFM analysts handle intraday changes and absences?


Intraday management covers the staffing adjustments a WFM analyst makes as conditions change throughout the day. To stay on top of it, the analyst tracks adherence to see how closely agents are following their schedules and compares actual contact volume against the forecast, interval by interval.


On the day of the carrier delay, that comparison shows the analyst by mid-morning that the afternoon’s staffing won’t cover the extra contacts. With a pre-built plan ready, they can send offers to both staffed and unstaffed agents in a few clicks, giving them the option to extend their shift or pick up an extra one. Off-shift agents receive the offer on their WFM app and can accept it from wherever they are.


The approach also works in reverse. On a slower day, the analyst can send voluntary time off (VTO) offers to the evening shift hours before it starts, keeping labor costs in line with demand.


Unexpected absences are part of intraday work too. If an agent gets a flat tire on the way in, they can check in late from the app, and both the WFM analyst and their supervisor see the update in real time without the need for a conversation. The analyst can then decide whether to cover the gap before the agent arrives.


## What’s a healthy agent occupancy rate during the holidays?


Occupancy measures how much of an agent’s logged-in time is spent handling customer contacts, including talk time and after-contact work. To calculate it, divide total handle time by total logged-in time, then multiply by 100.


The WFM analyst can track occupancy alongside adherence and volume. Contact centers[commonly cap occupancy at 85 to 90%](https://www.callcentrehelper.com/agent-occupancy-89603.htm) since agents above 90% have little time between contacts and face a higher risk of burnout. On the low end, occupancy below 70 to 75% can mean more agents are scheduled than the workload requires.


With customers still asking about their delayed gifts, the analyst might see afternoon occupancy around 90%, even after agents pick up extra hours. To ease the pressure, they can move agents who usually handle email onto live channels for a few hours, giving everyone additional time between contacts.


When agents have more idle time than expected, the analyst can fill it with off-queue work, like short refresher training sessions, or deploy more agents to channels like email if catch-up is needed.


## What lowers CSAT and agent performance during peak season?


At the end of the day, the team can review agent conversations to see what customers asked about and where interactions fell short. AI-powered conversation analytics can analyze every interaction and surface trends that a manual review of only a small interaction sample would miss.


Some trends may confirm what the team already knows, like the steady stream of questions about late orders. Others could be new, such as a cluster of customers confused about which items still qualify for a holiday promotion.


To find what’s lowering CSAT, look closely at repeat contacts and low-scoring conversations. If customers who asked about the delay reached out a second time, agents may have shared delivery estimates that weren’t specific enough. Long handle times on promotion questions may indicate a gap in the knowledge base. The analysis can also show which agents could use extra help, such as an agent whose billing conversations led to several escalations.


These findings become the agenda for tomorrow’s standup, where the team decides what to update and which agents to coach.


## How do I prevent agent burnout during the holidays?


Throughout the season, extended shifts and repetitive questions can wear agents down. Burnout can lead to more unplanned absences in December and higher turnover once the holidays end.


Flexible scheduling gives agents more control over when they work. Split shifts are one option, letting an agent work a morning block and an evening block with a few hours off in between for holiday errands or family commitments. The WFM analyst can build these options into the schedule while still covering the busiest intervals.


Planned breaks deserve safeguarding too. When the queue stays busy for hours at a time, agents may postpone breaks to keep up. The WFM analyst can schedule breaks in advance, and supervisors can make sure agents on their team step away when a break comes up, even on the busiest afternoons. In addition, modern WFM software enables the adjustment of breaks for different groups of agents in just a few clicks.


## What should a contact center do after the holidays?


In January, take time to review the season in depth while the details are still fresh. Compare the forecast with actual contact volume to see where it held up and where it missed, like the afternoon of the carrier delay. Note which AI agent answers and escalation rules needed the most adjustments during the season, since those are the first places to revisit when planning begins again. Perform a deeper dive into conversational data, especially with seasonal employees, to better understand agent capabilities for the coming year.


Each adjustment a contact center makes during the holiday season also helps with next year’s planning. The season’s contact volume and staffing data become history that AI-powered forecasting can learn from, ensuring the next holiday forecast starts from a more accurate baseline.
